analysis.one_liner: Cuts the new corporate minimum tax bill for large oil and gas drilling companies.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would lower the 15% corporate minimum tax owed by large oil and gas producers, was introduced by Senator Lankford with 7 Republican cosponsors and never received a committee hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2022, Congress created a 15% minimum tax on the book profits of the largest corporations. Oil and gas companies argued that drilling costs they can deduct for regular tax purposes still counted against their book income under the minimum tax, raising their bills. This bill would change the tax code so those drilling costs reduce the income the minimum tax applies to, directly lowering the tax owed by large energy producers. It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Large oil and gas companies subject to the corporate alternative minimum tax — the biggest corporations, not small drillers — would pay hundreds of millions less in federal taxes each year by deducting intangible drilling and development costs from the income the minimum tax applies to.

how_it_helps.text: Amends section 56A of the tax code so that deductions for intangible drilling and development costs (section 263(c)) reduce adjusted financial statement income, the base for the 15% corporate minimum tax [S2].
Also adjusts how depreciation and depletion expenses are treated under the minimum tax for drilling property, further reducing the tax base [S2].
Applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2022, reaching back to cover years already under the minimum tax [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury: every dollar of minimum tax the bill removes from oil and gas companies is a dollar not collected, which is ultimately made up by other taxpayers or added borrowing. Ordinary people get nothing direct in return.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers through lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill is a targeted tax cut for one industry with no offsetting revenue or benefit for anyone else; it lowers the tax base of the 15% corporate minimum tax enacted in 2022 specifically for drilling costs [S2].
It would reach back retroactively to tax years after December 31, 2022, rewarding companies for taxes already assessed under current law [S2].

Because only the largest corporations — those averaging over $1 billion in financial statement income — owe the minimum tax, the benefit flows to the biggest energy companies, not small operators (how the minimum tax works).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The entire benefit goes to a handful of the largest energy companies, and the entire cost is federal revenue that other taxpayers make up. The bill offers no consumer protection, no price relief mechanism, and no offset; it is a one-sided tax reduction dressed as a pro-domestic-energy measure. Its only honest defense is that companies should not pay tax on costs they deduct elsewhere in the code — but this bill resolves that tension only for the oil and gas industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Lankford introduced the bill on November 30, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1] [S4].
Seven Republican senators cosponsored the bill [S3].
No further action was ever recorded: the bill sat in the Finance Committee until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without a hearing, a markup, or a vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, large oil and gas corporations continue paying the 15% corporate minimum tax on drilling costs without the deduction this bill would have given them, and the federal treasury keeps the revenue. Nobody gained a benefit; the public was spared a targeted industry tax cut.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The treasury; oil companies gained nothing

for.name: Sen. James Lankford
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oklahoma; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee.

for.name: 7 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Daines, Barrasso, and Scott of South Carolina.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship and cosponsorship came from Republicans (the sponsor plus 7 cosponsors of 49 Senate Republicans); no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-led Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would let large drilling companies deduct intangible drilling and development costs from the income the 15% corporate minimum tax applies to, directly lowering their federal tax bills. The revenue loss is borne by general taxpayers, with no price relief or benefit passed to consumers.

industries.industry: Other large corporations subject to the minimum tax
industries.note: Companies outside oil and gas would continue paying the 15% minimum tax on their full book income while drilling companies get an exclusive carve-out, leaving them relatively worse off.
